messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mina Haddad, a 63-year-old single Middle Eastern woman who worked for years as an auditor, came to treatment months after her younger brother was taken hostage during a violent incident abroad and later found dead. The details of that day remained seared into her because she had first learned of the crisis by phone while he was on a work trip, then spent hours hearing fragments from relatives and officials before the confirmation came. What stayed with her most was not only the loss but the helplessness of waiting with no control, imagining where he might be, whether he was frightened, and whether anyone could reach him in time. Since then, Mina had found herself scanning for danger in ordinary life, sleeping lightly, and feeling as if her body never fully stood down.

Certain situations pulled her back with particular force. A locked conference room at her office could make her chest tighten before she even sat down, because the closed door and lack of an easy exit reminded her of her brother being trapped and unreachable; in those moments she became watchful, checking the handle, the windows, and who else was nearby. The same happened when she visited a wooded park near her apartment, where a trail, a patch of trees, or the smell of damp earth could suddenly make the present feel thin and unsafe, as if she were back in the same helpless uncertainty of the search. Even a news story, a photograph, or a family member mentioning victims in another context could jolt her into the same state, and she had come to dread these reminders because they seemed to arrive without warning. As she experienced those repeated surges, Mina began to believe that she could not trust the world to remain orderly or kind, and that if danger could strike her family once, it could strike again anywhere; she also felt betrayed by her own body, which reacted with racing alertness long after she knew she was safe.

Over time, Mina’s fear spread beyond the original reminders. She started avoiding unfamiliar places because, in her words, she could not assess the danger there, and she preferred routes, restaurants, and shops she knew well. At work she would accept only meeting rooms she had seen before, and she arranged her schedule so she would not have to arrive early at empty buildings or stay late after others had gone. That caution had practical consequences: she declined an assignment that would have required travel to a client site she had never visited, something she would once have taken pride in managing. The more she narrowed her world, the more she felt exposed to the possibility that bad things could happen without warning, and that sense of vulnerability deepened her belief that she had no way to stop them. She interpreted her own watchfulness as evidence that the danger was still near, and the constant monitoring made her feel even less secure.

The memories themselves intruded in a way Mina found unbearable. When they came, they did not arrive as a distant recollection but as a complete return of the event, with images, sounds, and bodily terror all at once: the phone ringing, voices speaking too fast, the stale air in the room where she waited, the sickening dread that her brother was somewhere suffering. Sometimes a smell in the office corridor or a sudden silence in her apartment could bring the whole scene back without warning, and she would freeze, gripped by the same terror she had felt at the time. On nights when she could not fall asleep or woke repeatedly, the memories were worse, and she lay listening for signs of danger, her mind replaying the hours of helpless waiting. In those moments she felt certain that her body was still reacting as if the crisis were ongoing, which made her more convinced that she was not truly safe.

Mina’s loss of faith in people, life, and even a higher power sat underneath much of this. She spoke quietly about how she no longer believed others would protect what mattered or that the world made moral sense, and that bleakness made her even more alert to possible threats. Because she expected danger and betrayal, places she could not fully read felt even riskier, and reminders of victims felt like proof that suffering could appear anywhere. Those same beliefs also made the memories more powerful: when she recalled her brother’s death, she did not just remember what happened, she felt confirmed in the idea that tragedy was random, unstoppable, and personally waiting for her. Mina had finally sought help when she realized she was spending more and more time avoiding places, sleeping poorly, and living as if she were always on guard, and what she most hoped for was some way to stop feeling that immediate surge of fear while also fearing that, if she let her guard down, another loss would catch her unprepared.
